news.2026-10-15-pont-yalou-coree-du-nord: Sinuiju and Dandong, on the Yalu River
China and North Korea finally open their new bridge, shut for twelve years
A four-lane bridge more than 3 kilometres long, finished on the Chinese side in 2014, took its first trucks on 15 October. It should ease congestion on the border between the two countries.

The New Yalu River Bridge, between Dandong (China) and Sinuiju (North Korea), opened on 15 October 2026: trucks flying the flags of both countries began driving in both directions late in the morning, according to AFP reporters [2].
It is a four-lane bridge about 3,026 metres long. China finished its part in 2014; officially, the North Korean side lacked access roads and customs facilities [2][3].

Until now, freight mostly crossed the old “Friendship Bridge”, built in 1943, which has only two lanes. Traders hope traffic will be spread out and that the volume of goods could nearly double, even though sanctions on Pyongyang limit what can really be traded there [2][3].

This bridge answers a simple question: by which route do goods reach a very isolated country? This corridor carries about 70% of trade between China and North Korea, so a second route really changes the capacity for trade [3].

The timing matters too: relations between Beijing and Pyongyang have warmed since 2018 and Xi Jinping visited Pyongyang in June [2]. The opening came a day after a submarine-launched cruise missile test announced by North Korea's KCNA agency [2]. North Korea's official news agency had not, at first, reported the opening [2].

You don't buy anything from North Korea, but this bridge shows how a country under sanctions keeps access to its giant neighbour. The more this door opens, the less Western sanctions weigh in practice.

news.2026-10-15-nord-stream-proces-hambo: Who blew up Nord Stream? A former Ukrainian soldier is on trial in Hamburg
The trial of the only defendant in the 2022 pipeline sabotage opened in Germany on 14 October. He denies the charges and remains silent.

The trial opened on Wednesday 14 October 2026 before the Higher Regional Court in Hamburg. The only defendant is Serhii K., a former Ukrainian soldier (also spelled Kuznetsov or Kuznietsov), charged with being an accomplice to a war crime, causing an explosion and destroying property; he faces up to 15 years in prison [1][2].

According to the prosecution, he entered Germany in September 2022 with a forged Ukrainian passport, then rented a yacht with six accomplices to plant the explosives. The indictment claims the operation was carried out on behalf of Ukrainian state agencies [1][2].

The defendant denies the charges, chose to stay silent in court, and his defence calls the evidence “circumstantial”: his fingerprints were not found on the yacht. He was arrested in Italy in August 2025, then sent to Germany; hearings are due to run until early next year [1][2][3].

This trial is the first to examine in court who destroyed the gas pipelines through which Russian gas reached Germany. Four years after the explosions, German justice is finally putting a name to the investigation, but only one man is on trial [1][3].

The case is also a test for the laws of war: can a soldier acting on orders be tried as a war criminal for targeting civilian infrastructure? And the German investigation points to an order from the Ukrainian state, a delicate subject for an ally of Berlin [1][2].

These pipelines long brought cheap Russian gas to Europe, and their destruction is part of what pushed energy bills up in 2022. Knowing who targeted them also means knowing whether undersea energy networks are protected.

news.2026-10-15-soudan-frappe-mine-or.ge: Northern Sudan, near the Egyptian border
news.2026-10-15-soudan-frappe-mine-or.ti: Sudan: an air strike on a gold mine near Egypt kills 72 people, according to an NGO
news.2026-10-15-soudan-frappe-mine-or.su: Sudan's army chief has opened an inquiry into a strike on 10 October near the border with Egypt. An organisation blames Cairo; Egypt has not commented.
news.2026-10-15-soudan-frappe-mine-or.po: On Saturday 10 October, an air strike hit a gold mining site in the Jabal al-Uqaydat area, near the Egyptian border, killing 72 people according to the organisation Emergency Lawyers, which accuses Egypt of being behind it [1][2].
On Monday 12 October, General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan set up an inquiry committee made up of judges, prosecutors and security representatives [1][2].
AFP could not verify these accusations. Egypt has made no official comment; its foreign minister called his Sudanese counterpart to stress respect for each country's territorial integrity [2].
news.2026-10-15-soudan-frappe-mine-or.wh: This area borders the Halaib Triangle, which both Sudan and Egypt claim: a strike on a gold mine there could turn an internal conflict into a crisis between two neighbouring countries [2].

The figures remain very uncertain: other groups, including the Umma Party, put the toll at 200, far above the 72 announced [3]. Until the inquiry reports its findings, the key point is that these are unproven accusations.
news.2026-10-15-soudan-frappe-mine-or.fo: Gold is a safe haven that many savers buy when the world gets worried. Part of it comes from small-scale mines, sometimes in war zones: every strike on a mining site is a reminder that the shiny metal also has a very concrete origin.

news.2026-10-15-egypte-canal-de-suez-sur: Egypt is building a “Suez Canal on rails” to link the Red Sea to the Mediterranean
Faced with disruption in the Red Sea, Cairo is betting on a 2,000 km high-speed line and eight logistics corridors. Its capacity will remain small next to the canal.
Egypt's Economy Minister, Ahmed Rostom, presents rail and infrastructure as a way for traders to move goods between the Red Sea and the Mediterranean [1].

The central project is an electrified high-speed line of about 2,000 km, estimated at 8.7 billion dollars and nicknamed “Suez Canal on Rails” [1]. Egypt has also started eight logistics corridors between the two seas [2].
The authorities expect about 15 million tonnes of freight a year, roughly 3% of the volume that went through the Suez Canal last year [3].

The idea is to stop depending on a single waterway. Shipping companies have avoided the Red Sea because of attacks, and Egypt, which partly lives off canal tolls, is looking for a way to keep goods on its territory [1].

It needs putting in perspective, though: 15 million tonnes is very little next to the canal [3]. Another outlet describes this train as a complement to the canal, not a replacement [4]. It is insurance, not a full alternative.
Much of what you buy online from Asia goes through Suez. When that route is blocked, journeys get longer and transport prices rise; every new route, even a small one, reduces that risk a little.

news.2026-10-15-rdc-kabila-front-rebelle: DR Congo: former president Kabila takes the lead of an armed movement replacing AFC/M23
Joseph Kabila chairs the new “Front for the Refoundation of the Nation”, announced in Goma on 12 October. The government has not yet reacted.
On 12 October 2026, in Goma, Joseph Kabila was named president of the Front pour la refondation de la nation (FRN), a political-military movement that succeeds the AFC/M23 alliance [1][2].
Corneille Nangaa and Bertrand Bisimwa are vice-presidents, and Sultani Makenga is chief of defence staff [1][3].

The movement says it wants to end what it calls “tyranny” by any means, including force. Kabila was sentenced to death in absentia a year ago for complicity with M23, which he has always denied; Félix Tshisekedi's government had not yet reacted [1][2].

A former head of state officially taking the lead of a rebellion is a turning point: the conflict in eastern Congo stops being only a matter of armed groups and becomes an open political confrontation with Kinshasa's authorities [1][2].
One unknown remains: the declaration does not clearly say what becomes of M23 as a movement [3]. It is one of the points to follow in the coming days.
Eastern Congo is a mining region whose metals end up in electronics. A hardening conflict adds uncertainty to those supplies, though the effect cannot be quantified at this stage.

news.2026-10-15-ormuz-cargo-coule-mine.t: Hormuz: the Revolutionary Guards say a cargo ship sank on a mine, a first in this war
news.2026-10-15-ormuz-cargo-coule-mine.s: Attacks in the strait are reportedly at a record level: 15 incidents logged between 6 and 14 October, 11 of them in four days. Macron is preparing a tour of the Gulf.
news.2026-10-15-ormuz-cargo-coule-mine.p: The UK centre UKMTO logged 15 attacks in the Strait of Hormuz between 6 and 14 October, 11 of them in the last four days [1].

Iran's Revolutionary Guards say a cargo ship sank after hitting a naval mine; it would be the first sinking of this kind reported since the start of the war. This is their account, not an independent finding [1].
Emmanuel Macron is due to visit Kuwait, the Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar from 19 to 21 October to discuss Hormuz and energy prices [2].
news.2026-10-15-ormuz-cargo-coule-mine.w: A mine is more dangerous than a shot: it stays in the water and threatens every ship, even long afterwards. That is why a sinking of this kind, if confirmed, weighs on insurers and shipowners well beyond the day of the incident [1].
The strait is a key route for Gulf oil. Each extra incident raises fears that flows will collapse again, as Al Jazeera's headline suggests [1].
news.2026-10-15-ormuz-cargo-coule-mine.f: When traffic drops in this strait, oil gets more expensive and it ends up at the pump and in transport bills. Macron's visit shows that Paris is genuinely worried.

news.2026-10-15-fmi-moyen-orient-recessi: The IMF expects the Middle East economy to shrink, with double-digit falls in Kuwait, Iraq, Qatar and Bahrain
The IMF now expects the Middle East and Central Asia to shrink by 0.3%, against 1.9% growth forecast six months ago, because Hormuz stays closed for longer.
In its October forecasts, the IMF says the economy of the Middle East and Central Asia will contract by 0.3% in 2026, whereas it had forecast 1.9% growth six months earlier [1][2].

It explains the change by a longer closure of the Strait of Hormuz than in its April scenario. Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain are the hardest hit: double-digit contractions in 2026, followed by double-digit rebounds in 2027 [1][3].
Saudi Arabia is expected to shrink by 3.3%, one of the least affected countries thanks to more varied export routes, but this forecast predates the recent attacks on Riyadh airport [1].
A shrinking economy in a region that sells the world its energy is rare: it shows how costly the war and the blocked strait are, even for very rich countries [1][3].
The IMF bets on a big rebound in 2027 provided the strait reopens. If the crisis lasts, these figures will be revised down: everything depends on the end of the conflict [1].
You won't see it in your wallet overnight, but a weakening region that produces so much oil and gas is a risk for energy prices and for French exports to the Gulf.

news.2026-10-15-alberta-referendum-separ: Alberta: Canada's oil province votes on Monday on the path to independence
On 19 October, Albertans answer ten questions. The last would only open the door to a future referendum, but oil and pipelines are at stake.

The referendum takes place on Monday 19 October 2026. Questions 1 to 9 are about public policy; question 10 asks whether the province should start the process towards a possible binding referendum on separation [1][3].

A “yes” would therefore not take Alberta out of Canada: it would only open the way to another referendum, after an assessment by Ottawa under the Clarity Act. Polls have long shown that independence is far from convincing the vast majority of Albertans [1][3].
Premier Danielle Smith defends a “sovereign Alberta within a united Canada”; Prime Minister Mark Carney calls it a “dangerous bluff” and compares it to Brexit [1][2].

Alberta sends more than two-thirds of its oil exports to the United States, and that crude often reaches American refineries through pipelines crossing other provinces. Analysts think a “yes” would not disrupt flows right away, but would raise lasting questions about transit, trade rules and investor confidence [3].

A University of Calgary study puts the initial cost of independence at between 50 and 170 billion dollars over five years [3]. The result will mostly show how much anger at Ottawa, notably over environmental rules, weighs at the ballot box [3].
Canada is a major oil supplier to its American neighbours. A political crisis there could one day weigh on crude prices and on North American trade agreements, where tariffs are already a hot topic.

culture.voiture-champ-de-bataille.title: Electric cars: a battle a century old
culture.voiture-champ-de-bataille.hook: In 1914, Henry Ford already wanted an electric Model T. Prices, subsidies, standards, pollution: what holds back electric cars today replays the conflicts that gave birth to the car.
culture.voiture-champ-de-bataille.tldr.0: The electric car is not new: ==Ford tried it in 1914==, and the battery was already what made it fail [1].
culture.voiture-champ-de-bataille.tldr.1: Today it costs ==much more to buy but less to run==, and the public subsidies that bridge the gap are expensive for the climate [2].
culture.voiture-champ-de-bataille.tldr.2: Luxury or mass market, angry customers, safety, pollution: ==the same conflicts keep coming back==, and low-income households risk losing out [1][2].

culture.voiture-champ-de-bataille.sectio: 1914: the battery, already
Before Tesla, there was the electric Model T.

In early 1914, Henry Ford, now the world's largest carmaker, announces an electric Model T. He sets aside land for the factory, builds a team, and a price of 500 dollars is even mentioned, almost that of the petrol version [1][3].
But the batteries from his friend Thomas Edison ==take a long time to charge, lack power and cost too much==. At the end of 1914, after spending 1.5 million dollars, Ford gives up [1][3].

A century later, the battery still weighs on the price. In 2022, an electric city car (Clio size) cost ==about 16,000 euros more to buy== than the same car with a petrol engine, but saved ==about 1,200 euros a year== in use [2].

Subsidies at the time covered half to all of the gap. As a result, going electric paid off right away for a small model bought by a very low-income household, but took about six years for a city car bought by a middle- or high-income household [2].
The forgotten detail
Batteries invented in France
The nickel-iron batteries of the electric Model T had been invented in France, then improved by Edison with several patents [1].
Luxury or mass market: the dilemma returns
"A business corporation is organized and carried on primarily for the profit of stockholders." Michigan Supreme Court, 1919 [1].
A car for everyone was not obvious. At first, ==expensive cars for a few wealthy buyers paid very large dividends==, and the average price of cars went up instead of down [1].

When Ford wants a popular car, his shareholders oppose it. In 1916, the Dodge brothers sue him to protect their dividends and win in 1919. Ford ends up buying all their shares. In Europe, carmakers long stick to small luxury runs [1].
The same dilemma weighs on electric cars: in 2022, they paid off right away for an SUV, much less for a city car. And the only clearly identified new entry-level model was made in China [2].
Customers who fought back
The first cars broke down, fell apart, caught fire. Customers sued.

Early cars often broke down, fell apart and caught fire. According to historian Sally Clarke, many American customers went to court: against garages, who sued carmakers, who blamed the dealers. Little by little, ==the courts imposed heavy fines== [1].
Even the Model T was not perfect: it was mainly better than other cars at its price [1].

Today, distrust has changed form: ==uncertainty about electricity prices and the number of charging points holds back purchases==, even though electric cars are cheaper to run. And at a public fast charger, charging costs three to four times more than at home [2].
Archive document · 1925
"A very bad deal"
In 1925, the head of the Banque de l'Indochine branch in Tientsin, China, writes to Paris: his 1921 Renault 18 HP limousine goes to the garage almost every month and burns 28 litres per 100 km [1].
He asks to replace it with a Peugeot 15 HP, which uses only about 15 litres. The garage that sold him the Renault agrees to take it back, to make amends [1].
Expensive subsidies, and people left behind
Those who will most need to change cars are those with the least access to electric ones.

Even assuming an electric car runs for sixteen years, purchase subsidies cost ==at least 300 euros of public money per tonne of CO2 avoided==, not counting the higher emissions from building the battery [2].

Low-income households mostly buy second-hand, where electric cars are still rare: in 2019, ==only 0.3% of the cars owned by the poorest 10% of households were electric==. Yet low-emission zones will gradually ban older cars from big cities [2].
Who will pay, who will build?
For Patrick Fridenson, the car has always been "technopolitical": an object shaped by conflicts between carmakers, shareholders, customers, garages, insurers, elected officials and experts [1].

The France Stratégie authors suggest keeping the bonus for small electric cars, toughening the penalty on emissions and weight, helping low-income households with long-term leasing, and giving clarity on electricity and charging points. These are policy ideas, not the government's position [2].
Then there is industry: ==most electric cars bought in France are made abroad==, so subsidies do little for French factories [2].

culture.voiture-champ-de-bataille.sectio: Drivers versus experts: who made the car safer?
The car became safer because of the damage it caused.

For the American historian Lee Vinsel, road safety was born from ==a permanent conflict between drivers, carmakers and experts==. Every new technology creates new dangers, and so new rules. And those rules go beyond the car: roads, city traffic, road signs, petrol pumps all form one system [1].

From the 1920s, ==American insurers== studied accidents and hired experts to put figures on them and share out responsibility. In the 1950s and 1960s they launched research into what makes a car sturdy and stable; in 1959 they created a non-profit road safety research institute [1].

Government agencies are not referees that fell from the sky: according to Vinsel, ==they were demanded by the people living through the car's crises==. Rules came out of meetings between carmakers, elected officials (city, state and federal) and administrations [1].

Targeting only the most dangerous drivers was not enough. So standards were created so that the car would no longer be a "coffin on wheels". These standards were not only about mass production: ==customers and their lawyers demanded them too==, and from the 1920s carmakers' design offices were looking for more reliable cars [1].
In France, road equipment long served first of all to ==protect pedestrians==, before people gradually learned to share the road, according to the historian Mathieu Flonneau [1].

The danger of exhaust fumes was known very early: ==the first manuals advised against running the engine in a closed room==, because of carbon monoxide. But urban air pollution only became an issue with the Los Angeles smog in the 1950s; before that, coal smoke was the worry. For the American public, the big problem remained accidents [1].
Another little-known fact: safety gained momentum in the United States, but ==the first initiatives against car pollution came from far from the big car capitals==, for example from Sweden [1].
Pollution is now central: in 2021, transport accounted for 30% of France's greenhouse gas emissions, the only sector still above its 1990 level [2].
The forgotten detail · 1966
"Cars that kill", a softened version

In 1965, the American lawyer Ralph Nader published a shocking book on dangerous cars. It was translated very quickly in France, by two women, under a more radical title: "Ces voitures qui tuent" ("These cars that kill", 1966) [1].

But the publisher added "technical notes" by the motoring journalist Roger Brioult: French cars were supposedly safer, and many problems came from drivers themselves. According to the historian Patrick Fridenson, these notes ==very probably came from an intervention by the carmakers' trade association== with the publisher [1].
